# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-34 (Extended v221)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 9. Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Marseilles, Naples, Elba, El Giglio island. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven.

## English Subplot Summary

**Established facts through summer Year 9**: Multiple residents migrated between villages. Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Solemn promises: Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe.

**Chapter 33-34 domestic observations**: Pelde Stenson, Dalis Stenworth, Davus, Rimor Corrford, Kassa Brackick, Volan Stenworth tired or aching. Yera Stenworth sorted old letters, hummed tune while scrubbing step, read almanac mispronouncing saints. Istho Stenworth hummed tune while scrubbing step, counted coins twice (came up penny short), asked if it would rain (Isric shrugged). Luvie Prydenridge bought ribbon (regretted it), hummed tune while scrubbing step, discussed salt prices scandal. Istho, Jotho, Nerine predicted rain (wrongly). Jotho mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Rozek Stenenridge fell asleep before fire. Lurald remarked river up; Yera said it always was in spring. Luvie told Rozek old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. Luvie and Semor Brackick argued with carter over oats price. Smoke lay flat; gulls quarreled over fish heads. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Rain threatened but held off. Baker's boy late. Bells rang thinly. Children chased hoop. Salt prices discussed as scandalous. Kassa counted coins twice (came up penny short). Only son of Luena Stenenridge packed single trunk, moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth took Sebin Brackick in marriage at Torton before autumn was out; couple lived in Torton from then on.

**Chapter 34 updates**: Kassa Brackick spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood. Volan asked if it would rain; Kassa shrugged. Kassa remarked river is up again; Volan said it always was in spring. Pelde Stenworth mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Harine Lindmere and Dalis talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Baker's boy late again; line at oven grew long. Frost silvered hedges overnight. Elra watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Elra Corrford watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Fewyn Stenworth packed single trunk and moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby. Elra counted coins twice and came up penny short. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Elra mended torn sleeve by window and said little. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar.

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent.

**Barricade and rescue (June Year 6)**: Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Marius witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery (7 September)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. When Marius called grandfather "father" three times, Gillenormand agreed to bring Cosette.

**Cosette's arrival and revelation**: Learned she was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. **Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown.**

**Wedding (1 February 1833, church of Saint-Paul)**: **Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath.** Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. First coach held Cosette, Aunt Gillenormand, M. Gillenormand, Jean Valjean. Marius came in second coach. **During dinner, Basque reported M. Fauchelevent injured hand paining him; begged excuse; would come tomorrow. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Jean Valjean's moral crisis post-wedding**: In Cosette's empty bedroom: no sheets, pillow without case. All feminine objects removed. Only Jean Valjean's bed made up. Remained twelve long hours ice-cold, motionless as corpse. Then shuddered convulsively, kissed Cosette's garments.

**Javert's death (evening, Place du Châtelet)**: Took off hat, placed on quay edge. Tall black figure appeared on parapet, bent towards Seine, drew self up, fell straight down. Dull splash followed. Javert drowned. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade, heard frightful pistol shot behind Rue Mondétour.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and estrangement (17 February morning)**: Very pale, eyes hollow, sunken by sleeplessness. **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Justified: conscience implacable; duty places one in hell. Marius shocked, pleaded with him not to tell Cosette: "She does not know, it would terrify her." Jean Valjean chose to tell himself—nothing forced him.

**Marius's rationalization**: Concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Dung-heap aids spring to create rose. Adored Cosette, she is light. Jean Valjean is empty chrysalis. Convict appeared hideous, repulsive. Must keep word promised to Jean Valjean. First duty to Cosette. Acquired knowledge of six hundred thousand francs. Unable to probe out of respect for promised secret. Believed grave duty: restitution to someone sought with discretion. Abstained from touching money meanwhile.

**Cosette's alienation**: Address as _thou_ replaced by _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean," rendering him another person. She became more gay, less tender. Still loved him sincerely. One day chanced to say "father." Flash of joy illuminated his melancholy countenance. He caught her up: "Say Jean."—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean" with laughter. **"That is right," said he. Turned aside to wipe eyes. This was the last time.** Complete extinction ensued. No more familiarity, no more good-morning with kiss. After losing Cosette wholly in one day, afterwards obliged to lose her again in detail.

**Marius's estrangement strategy**: Before marriage, put no questions to M. Fauchelevent; since marriage, feared to put any to Jean Valjean. Confined himself to gradually estranging Jean Valjean from house and effacing him from Cosette's mind. More than effacement, it was eclipse. All-powerful magnetism caused Cosette to do instinctively what Marius wished. She conformed to Marius' will regarding "Monsieur Jean," heedlessly not remembering what Marius forgot. **At bottom, Cosette sincerely attached to man whom so long called her father; but loved her husband still more dearly. This had somewhat disturbed balance of her heart, which leaned to one side only.**

**Jean Valjean's withdrawal (late spring/summer 1833)**: Old man neatly clad in black emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. Passed Blancs-Manteaux, gained Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, reached Rue de l'Écharpe, turned left into Rue Saint-Louis. Soon went only as far as Rue Pavée, shook head, turned back. Then did not overstep Blancs-Manteaux. Head craned forward; chin moved; folds in gaunt neck painful to behold. Sometimes had umbrella but never opened it. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** What he bore on brow was no longer wrinkles of age, but mysterious mark of death. Cheeks pendulous; skin had color leading one to think earth already upon it; corners of mouth drooped as in mask ancients sculptured on tombs. Gazed into space with air of reproach.

**Physical collapse**: Week passed: Jean Valjean had not taken a step in room, remained in bed. Portress said old man does not get up, no longer eats, will not last long. Made effort to dress in old workingman's clothes, obliged to pause many times. One day descended staircase, took three steps in street, seated himself on post, went upstairs. This was last oscillation of pendulum. Following day did not leave apartment. Day after that, did not leave bed.

**Preparations for death**: Took Bishop's candlesticks from chimney-piece, took two wax candles from drawer, put them in candlesticks. Lighted them though broad daylight, summer time. Forced to write with back of pen. **[Lamentable cries heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more. She is a smile which passed over me. I am about to plunge into night without even seeing her again. Oh! one minute, one instant, to hear her voice, to touch her dress, to gaze upon her, the angel! and then to die! What is frightful is to die without seeing her. She would smile on me, she would say a word to me. Here I am all alone. My God! My God! I shall never see her again!"**

**Marius and Cosette's discovery and invitation**: By accident, Marius learned all Jean Valjean had done. Told Jean Valjean: "Your chamber still stands ready in our house." Insisted Jean Valjean part of themselves; he is Cosette's father and Marius's. Shall not pass another day in dreadful house.

**Cosette's plea**: "If you only knew how pretty the garden is now! The azaleas are doing very well there. The walks are sanded with river sand; there are tiny violet shells. You shall eat my strawberries. I water them myself. And no more 'madame,' no more 'Monsieur Jean,' we are living under a Republic, everybody says _thou_, don't they, Marius? The programme is changed. If you only knew, father, I have had a sorrow, there was a robin redbreast which had made her nest in a hole in the wall, and a horrible cat ate her... You are going to come with us. How delighted grandfather will be! You shall have your plot in the garden, you shall cultivate it. And, then, I shall do everything that you wish, and then, you will obey me prettily."

**Jean Valjean's response**: Claims Death is good arrangement; God knows better what we need. May Marius have Cosette, may youth wed morning, may lilacs and nightingales surround them, may life be beautiful sunny lawn. Now let him die; all is right. Last night drank whole jug of water. Cosette much better off with husband. "Even if you were to take possession of me, Monsieur Pontmercy, would that make me other than I am? No, God has thought like you and myself, and he does not change his mind; it is useful for me to go."

**Final strength and revelation**: **All at once rose to his feet with firm step, detached from wall little copper crucifix suspended there, returned to seat with freedom of movement of perfect health, laid crucifix on table, spoke in loud voice.** Explained Cosette's fortune truly belongs to her: "What has pained me, Monsieur Pontmercy, is that you have not been willing to touch that money. That money really belongs to your wife." **Black jet comes from England, white jet comes from Norway. For bracelets, invented way of substituting for slides of soldered sheet iron, slides of iron laid together. It is prettier, better and less costly. Six hundred thousand francs made from this trade. Managed very well with glass goods rivalling Berlin jewellery. Could not equal black glass of England. A gross containing twelve hundred well-cut grains costs three francs.** Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette. My life will have been wasted if you do not enjoy them!"

**Final decline**: His breath became intermittent; little rattling interrupted it. Found difficulty in moving forearm, feet had lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb and feebleness of body increased, all majesty of soul displayed and spread over brow. Light of unknown world already visible in eyes.

## Thénardier's Blackmail Attempt and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and visit**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. Discovered man encountered in Grand Sewer. Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** Marius replied with cold tone, double "I know it."

**Thénardier's exposure and humiliation**: With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat. **Strangely surprised; bewildered nonetheless.** Baron recognized him thoroughly. Thénardier never seen Marius before.

**Marius's knowledge and confrontation**: **Revealed Javert's suicide facts**: Announced two newspapers: _Moniteur_ of 15th June, 1832, announced Javert's suicide, adding that Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof.**

**Marius's speech to Thénardier**: **"You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain. You came to accuse that man, you have only justified him; you wanted to ruin him, you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital. I know enough about you to send you to the galleys and even further if I choose. Here are a thousand francs, bully that you are! Of a Colonel! I wouldn't give a ha'penny for a general. Go! disappear! Only be happy, that is all that I desire. Ah! monster! here are three thousand francs more. Take them. You will depart to-morrow, for America, with your daughter; for your wife is dead, you abominable liar. I shall watch over your departure, you ruffian, and at that moment I will count out to you twenty thousand francs."**

**Thénardier's outcome**: **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**

## Père-Lachaise Cemetery

**Jean Valjean's burial location**: In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, in vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, far from all tombs of fancy, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone. Stone no more exempt than others from leprosy of time, dampness, lichens, defilement of birds. Water turns it green, air blackens it. Not near any path; people not fond of walking in that direction because grass high and feet immediately wet. When there is little sunshine, lizards come thither. All around quivering of weeds. In spring, linnets warble in trees.
